 Early voting in Maine surpasses last midterm election
 More Democrats, independents have voted early than Republicans
 By 
 Emma Davis 
 - 
 November 2, 2026 3:20 pm 
 The line to vote on the last day of early, in-person voting stretches the entire second floor of Portland City Hall on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
 People stood in a line that stretched across the entire second floor of Portland City Hall on the last day of early, in-person voting on Thursday, waiting at times more than an hour to cast their ballots in the midterm election that will decide three congressional seats, the governorship and every seat in the state Legislature.   
 “Good for us,” one voter remarked.  
 Early voting numbers have surpassed the last midterm election in 2022 and are approaching those from the 2024 presidential election. Also, far more voters have cast early ballots in-person than have mailed back absentee ballots, a continuation of a trend seen in recent years.  
 As of the latest data from Friday, 290,382 voters had voted early, which includes accepted returned absentee ballots and early votes in the presence of a clerk.  
 In 2022, 236,977 absentee ballots were returned and accepted through Election Day. In 2024, it was 378,764. 
 This year so far, more than 55% of early votes have been cast in-person. Nearly as many Mainers have voted in the presence of a clerk this year than at this point in 2024, and far more than in 2022.  
 While the percentage of people dropping absentee ballots in a drop box or with their clerk is about the same as 2024, and down slightly from 2022, the share of voters mailing ballots has decreased significantly — down about 8% from 2022 to 2024 and another 9% from 2024 to 2026. 
 Thursday also marked the last day to request an absentee ballot. This election, 323,562 absentee ballots have been requested, compared to 388,815 in 2024 and 252,702 in 2022.  
 Democrats have cast more early ballots than Republicans, about 47% to almost 23% out of all accepted ballots. Voters who are not enrolled with any political party have also cast more than Republicans, just over 27%.  
 This is fairly typical compared with years past.  
 There are about 3% fewer Democratic absentee ballot requests compared with 2022, but Democratic requests are up about 5% compared to the 2024 makeup. Requests from unenrolled voters are up more than 4.5% from 2022 and by about 1.5% from 2024. Meanwhile, Republican requests are down a little more than 1% from 2022 and down by about 5% from 2024. 
 “There’s nothing hugely surprising about this data,” Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said, noting that historically more Democrats vote early than Republicans. “What’s most exciting about the data is the level of enthusiasm.” 
 Noting that the primary election in June saw record turnout, Bellows said she is “optimistic that the excellent absentee numbers indicate a strong turnout.” She predicts 70% of all eligible voters will participate in the midterms, which would fall between turnout levels of 2022 and 2024.
